t0: 2003-08-14 14:14 EDT (FirstEnergy control-room alarms begin failing silently)

sources.title: U.S.-Canada Power System Outage Task Force, Final Report on the August 14, 2003 Blackout in the United States and Canada (April 2004)
What Really Happened During the 2003 Blackout? (Practical Engineering, 2022), summarizing the Task Force report
The 2003 Northeast Blackout--Five Years Later (Scientific American, 2008)
New York City Blackout of 2003 (NYCdata, Baruch College CUNY)
MIT OCW 6.691 Seminar in Electric Power Systems: The August 2003 Blackout (lecture notes citing Task Force analysis of 1,500 MW load shed)

points.event: 14:14 FE EMS alarms begin failing; operators unaware
15:05 Harding-Chamberlin 345 kV line trips (tree contact); first contingency violation
15:41 Star-South Canton trips (time from report; snippet not seen)
16:05:57 Sammis-Star trips; point of no return per Task Force
cascade completes across 8 states + Ontario, about 50-55 million people; commonly dated 16:10-16:13

threat.notes: extent = share of the eventual ~50 million affected people who have lost power. The threat is flat for ~1.9 h, then goes 1% -> 100% in roughly 7 minutes. The 16:10-16:13 end-of-cascade time and the 16:06 1% value are from memory of the Task Force report and Wikipedia, not seen verbatim in a snippet; the 15:32 and 15:41 line-trip times are also unconfirmed. Confirmed by snippets: 14:14 alarm loss, 15:05 Harding-Chamberlin, cascade after ~16:05, ~50 million people.

fragments.had: knowledge that the EMS/alarm servers were failing
fragments.notes: 14:20 EMS remote sites then core servers fail; IT worked on it but did not tell operators
realized ~15:42-15:45 that alarms/EMS were not working

fragments.had: state estimator: the tool that would show the contingency picture
fragments.notes: state estimator faulty from 12:15, back to full function 16:04

fragments.had: observations of line trips and flows at the FE boundary; called FE
fragments.notes: calls documented in the report; exact times not confirmed

fragments.who: the fix itself (Task Force post-hoc analysis)
fragments.had: shed ~1,500 MW of Cleveland-Akron load before 16:06
fragments.notes: applicable after 15:05, window closed at 16:06: about 1 hour

aggregation.notes: Derived from documented fragment-awareness times (hours after 14:14): FE IT aware 0.1 h (p10), FE operators aware ~1.5 h (median), MISO state estimator restored 1.83 h (p90). These are LOWER BOUNDS: the pieces never actually assembled into the 1,500 MW load-shed decision before the 16:06 point of no return (t=1.87). The window to act was ~1 hour (15:05-16:06).

deploy.notes: Not prevention: time from cascade to full restoration of New York City (9:03 pm Aug 15, ~29 h). Most areas were back within ~7 h, some places took up to 4 days (s3). The preventive load shed itself would have taken minutes (unsourced, not used).

ai_counterfactual.basis: Illustrative assumption. The fragments were all machine-readable signals already inside control rooms (EMS server health, line-trip telemetry, neighbor calls). Joining them into 'alarms are dead + lines are tripping + shed load' is a sub-1-hour human-expert reading task, well inside the ~17.4-hour 50%-success task horizon in RATES.md (METR time horizon, May-Aug 2026 entry). We assume ~15 min from the 14:14 alarm loss to a flagged, routed warning to FE operators; humans still decide and shed load. This would sit ~50 min before the first contingency (15:05) rather than after the point of no return. No claim that this would certainly have prevented the blackout.
ai_counterfactual.label: illustrative

gap_summary: The pieces needed ~1.5 h just to notice each other and never assembled; the cascade went from 1% to 100% of 50 million people in about 7 minutes once the 1-hour window closed.
